issues.legal_issue: Potential building-site value may be included in market value only when objective evidence shows that the potential can be realized within a reasonably near future.
material_facts: The acquired grove land was outside a town, abutted a main road, and was next to a school.
There was evidence of a few houses on nearby grove land, but no substantial building activity near the acquired land and no ascertainable trend of town development toward it.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not establish building-site potential that could be used as a basis for valuing the land.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value reflects the land’s existing advantages and potential possibilities, but potential must be objective and capable of being turned to account within a reasonably near future. Whether building potential exists depends on the overall evidence, including building pressure, suitability, direction and pace of development, and nearby construction. The Court relied on South Eastern Rail Co. v. L.C.C. and N. B. Jeejabhoy v. The District Collector, Thana.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.no_substantial_nearby_building_activity: There was no substantial building activity in the neighbourhood of the acquired land.
predicates.no_ascertainable_development_toward_land: There was no ascertainable trend of development toward the acquired land.

issues.definition: When a land-acquisition compensation case has neither substantial nearby building activity nor ascertainable development toward the land, building-site potential is not a basis for valuation.

issues.legal_issue: A genuine and unchallenged offer by a prospective purchaser may provide a better basis for land valuation than annual income from the land when another valuation method is available.
material_facts: A prospective purchaser testified that he had offered to buy the grove land to build a residence there.
The trial court accepted the offer as genuine and bona fide.
The offer evidence was not challenged as fabricated, excessive, non-bona-fide, made under compulsion, or made in special circumstances.
The High Court rejected the offer evidence and valued the land by estimating and capitalizing its annual income, although the grove had not reached maximum yield.
issues.conclusion: The offer was relevant valuation evidence, and there was no valid reason to reject the trial court’s acceptance of it in favour of the annual-income method; the trial court’s valuation was restored.
issues.legal_principle: An offer is relevant evidence of the prospective purchaser’s opinion of value, though it is not equivalent to a completed sale. Evidence that an owner rejected an offer shows only that the owner considered the land worth more, or had another reason for refusing. Annual produce value is an inadequate method where the owner may not have put the land to its best use or the land has not reached maximum yield; that method should be used only when no alternative method is available. The Court relied on Government of Bombay v. Merwanji Muncherji and Governor-General in Council v. Ghiasuddin.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_case and prospective_buyer_testified_to_offer and offer_evidence_was_unchallenged and not exceptional_purchase_pressure and alternative_valuation_method_available

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.prospective_buyer_testified_to_offer: A prospective purchaser testified to an offer that the purchaser had made to buy the land.
predicates.offer_evidence_was_unchallenged: The opposing side did not challenge the offer as non-genuine, excessive, or otherwise not bona fide.
predicates.exceptional_purchase_pressure: The prospective purchaser made the offer under compulsion or other exceptional pressure.
predicates.alternative_valuation_method_available: Evidence of a valuation method other than annual income from the land was available.

issues.definition: When a prospective purchaser testified to an unchallenged offer without exceptional purchase pressure in a land-acquisition compensation case, and another valuation method was available, the offer evidence should be used instead of annual-yield valuation.

issues.legal_issue: When a court exercises its discretion to award interest on excess compensation under a rule prescribing a single rate, it must award interest at that rate.
material_facts: The trial court awarded interest on the excess compensation but set a rate below the rate specified in the applicable provision.
The High Court considered the rate issue and held that the court could award interest at any rate up to the specified rate.
The applicable provision had not been amended to provide a variable rate.
issues.conclusion: The court’s discretion was whether to award interest; once it awarded interest, it had to use the prescribed rate.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as applicable in the case, gave the court discretion to award or refuse interest but required interest on the excess compensation at six per cent per annum if awarded. The Court compared section 28 with section 34, noting the same fixed-rate wording, and referred to state amendments that expressly provided different or variable rates. In the absence of such an amendment, the fixed rate applied.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.court_chooses_to_award_interest: The court exercises its discretion to award interest on excess compensation.
predicates.governing_interest_rule_prescribes_a_sin: The applicable interest rule specifies one rate rather than giving the court discretion to select a rate.

issues.definition: When a court awards interest in a land-acquisition compensation case and the governing rule specifies a single rate, the award must use that rate.

issues.legal_issue: A pure question of law may be considered for the first time by a court of last resort when it turns on construction or on facts admitted or proved beyond controversy.
material_facts: The appellant challenged the rate of interest in the court of last resort although the rate issue had not been specifically raised in the cross-objections below.
The High Court had in fact considered and decided the rate issue.
The question turned on the construction of the applicable provision, rather than on a disputed factual finding.
issues.conclusion: There was no bar to considering the rate-of-interest point, and it was proper to entertain it.
issues.legal_principle: A question of law first raised in a court of last resort may be entertained when it concerns construction of a document or rests on facts admitted or proved beyond controversy. The Court relied on Connecticut Fire Insurance Co. v. Kavanagh.

predicates.appeal_before_court_of_last_resort: The proceeding is an appeal before a court of last resort.
predicates.pure_question_of_law: The newly raised point concerns a question of law rather than a disputed factual issue.
predicates.question_depends_only_on_construction_or: The point depends only on construing a document or on facts admitted or proved beyond controversy.

issues.definition: In an appeal before a court of last resort, a new legal point that depends only on construction or undisputed facts may be considered.
